I have no issue with budget builds. For some people it's the only way to get into a PC to run the games they want to play. What I do take issue with is overselling the features of these builds. Words like "awesome", "excellent" and even "great" do not apply to most budget builds. "Acceptable", "adequate", and "sufficient" do. A 500W power supply is not "powerful" and should not be accompanied by a suggestion to users that they'll be able to upgrade whatever they want later on and still have plenty of power to draw from. Nobody talks about 720p as being high definition anymore, and so it's disappointing that someone would recommend a GPU claiming it will be able to render games at 1280x720 high definition. Technically it's accurate, but practically it's disingenuous.

And don't even get me started on the practical benefits of a PC with only one HD for storage @ 160GB. That's not even funny.

A lot of these builds are gimmick builds. They involve someone sitting down with a target budget and seeing if they can get all the critical components in a case for that amount. If they do manage to make it all work, they try to talk it up like it's something it isn't. Step 1 (assemble a PC on a strict budget) is great. Step 2 (make it sound better than it is) is what I have issue with. Misleading people to convince them that you've helped them more than you have is not cool.

The guy who buys a $250 rig on the promise that he could upgrade later is going to shit a brick when he finds out he needs a new case to accommodate the new GPU he bought. Then he's going to shit another brick when he realizes that the game he bought the new GPU to play wants 1/4 of his hard drive space and he needs to buy a new drive to make it all fit. And then he's going to eat those bricks and shit them again when the GPU kills his power supply and cooks his new HDD on its way out. Now his "great" $250 gaming PC with $300 in a new GPU has cost him an extra $250 in necessary (and unexpected) upgrades to support everything properly.

That's not a good deal.

Let's be real you aren't going to upgrade from a 610 to 390x. [500W is plenty for any midrange system] (http://www.anandtech.com/bench/GPU15/1240). Shit, I had an OC'ed i3 and a 6950 running for years on 450W, and that isn't exactly a power sipper. If you're going with no name brands then yeah you want a lot of headroom cause their wattage claims are bullshit. But that EVGA supply is quite good and will deliver what it says.

That said, the choices here are weird. A 610 is barely better than the iGPU. This budget would be one of the few times I'd recommend AMD over Intel. Taking the GPU money and getting an A-10 would get you waaaay better performance.

I think it's important to evaluate what I said in the context that I said it. The author described the 500W PSUs he favored in at least the first few builds as "powerful". It's not. It's adequate. 750-800W is powerful. My point is not that any one component the author mentioned is 'bad', per se, but that he's overselling them. If you want to get the best most reliable, stable, durable performance out of a PSU, you don't run it anywhere near its rated maximum, and 500W doesn't allow the kind of overhead you need to feel confident that your components are safe. You may have had great success with a 450W PSU but that doesn't mean everyone else will.

I'd rather someone who puts together an article like this be enthusiastic but dead honest about the builds. "For $250 you'll be getting the bare minimum and you'll find that trying to upgrade one thing may require you to upgrade some other things along with it in order to make it work. If you want a little more future-proofing and flexibility you might want to take a look at the $500 contender we've put together a little further along."
